passage:
Hansa, sit with your Dada. You look the way I looked at fifteen, before my board exams.
Back then I would lie on the roof and think, if only I were six again. At six I flew kites all day, no books, no marks. Life was one long holiday, I told myself.
Then one evening my mother heard me moaning about it. She laughed. "Santosh, at six you were terrified of the dark. You cried every night the power went. And you begged to cross the road alone, and I never let you."
I had forgotten all of it. The kite days were true, but so was the dark.
I'm not saying exams are easy. I'm saying the old days weren't only kites. Now, show me which chapter is giving you trouble.

qa.q: What did Santosh's mother remind him he was scared of at six?
qa.a: The dark; he cried every night the power went.

qa.q: Why did fifteen-year-old Santosh long to be six again?
qa.a: With board exams pressing, the kite-flying days felt like one long holiday, a comfort compared with books and marks.

qa.q: How does Dada turn the memory into help for Hansa?
qa.a: He admits exams are hard, shows the past had its own fears, then moves straight to the difficult chapter, so the pressure gets tackled instead of escaped.

qa.q: What might Santosh's mother have been thinking when she laughed?
qa.a: She probably found it sweet and a little funny, since she remembered the nightly tears and the limits he had forgotten.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a pressured teenager, he longed for carefree childhood until his mother reminded him of its fears and limits.

passage:
The power went out at nine, with Zeenat's project due at midnight and the laptop on eleven percent.
Zeenat lit the emergency lamp and flopped onto the bed. Across the room, Dilnaz, her eight-year-old sister, was happily colouring by lamplight.
"You're so lucky," Zeenat said. "I'd give anything to be eight. No deadlines. Just crayons and cartoons."
Dilnaz looked up. "I have a spelling test tomorrow. And I can't reach the top shelf. And you won't let me walk to the shop alone."
"That's different."
"And I'm scared of the dark," Dilnaz added, edging her lamp closer.
Zeenat remembered, suddenly, hiding under a blanket during power cuts at that age, heart thumping.
She sat up, opened the laptop, dimmed the screen, and typed the conclusion first.

qa.q: How much battery did Zeenat's laptop have when the power went out?
qa.a: Eleven percent, with the project due at midnight.

qa.q: Why does Zeenat wish she were eight again tonight?
qa.a: The deadline and the power cut make her feel trapped, so childhood looks like only crayons and cartoons, without the fears she once had. 😅

qa.q: What sensible step does Zeenat take once she stops wishing?
qa.a: She dims the screen to save battery and writes the conclusion first, working with the time and power she actually has.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see being eight?
qa.a: To Dilnaz, eight comes with its own worries: a spelling test, shelves out of reach, rules about the shop, and fear of the dark.

grounding: A teenager under deadline pressure envies her little sister's carefree age until the sister's own fears remind her what childhood was like.

passage:
Between school and evening coaching, Sonali had exactly forty minutes. She spent them on the floor of the Andheri flat, flipping through an old photo album.
There she was at five, chocolate on her chin, grinning at a birthday party. "Look at me," she said to Saurabh, her older brother, who was eating toast in the doorway. "Not a single worry. Why can't life be like that again?"
Saurabh leaned over and turned the page. Sonali, same age, howling on the edge of a swimming pool, clutching the rail.
"You screamed through every lesson that summer," he said. "And you cried when Mummy wouldn't let you go to the park without her."
Sonali frowned at the photo. She had forgotten the pool entirely.
"Still," she said, "it looks easier."
"Some of it was," Saurabh said. "Your bag's by the door."
She closed the album gently, not quite ready to put it away.

qa.q: What was Sonali doing in the swimming pool photo?
qa.a: Howling on the edge of a swimming pool, clutching the rail.

qa.q: Why does Sonali want life to be like it was at five?
qa.a: Squeezed between school and coaching, she longs for the carefree feeling in the birthday photo; the album is a comfort from the pressure.

qa.q: What could help Sonali with the pressure itself, not just the longing?
qa.a: Telling her family how packed her days feel and finding small breaks now, instead of looking for ease only in the past.

qa.q: How does Saurabh see Sonali's 'not a single worry' claim?
qa.a: Saurabh remembers the screaming at swimming lessons and the park rules, so he sees her early years as happy but not worry-free.

grounding: A busy teenager longs for her early childhood through photos, forgetting its fears until her brother turns the page.

passage: "Asif bhai, do you remember when I was five? No tests, no coaching, just the swing in the colony park." "I remember." "I'd give anything to go back. I was so happy then." "Irawati, you cried every night because you thought a ghost lived in the water tank." "...That was only sometimes." "You weren't allowed to cross the road. You weren't allowed near the stove. You screamed at the dentist so loudly the whole clinic heard." "Okay, okay." "And you begged to be big like me." "Did I?" "Every day. 'When will I be big, bhai?'" "Hmm. Maybe I just miss nobody expecting anything from me." "That part's real. The rest I think you've painted over." Ammi called from the kitchen, "Both of you, chai." Irawati smiled a little. "Fine. Big girls drink chai.

qa.q: What did Irawati think lived in the water tank when she was small?
qa.a: A ghost; she cried every night because of it.

qa.q: What is Irawati really missing when she says she wants to be five again?
qa.a: She misses a time when nobody expected anything from her, which feels very comforting under the pressure of tests and coaching.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation for Irawati?
qa.a: When Asif reminded her that she begged to be big, she saw that she was only remembering the easy parts and named what she actually missed.

qa.q: How might Asif feel listening to his sister wish to be five again?
qa.a: He seems caring but honest; he wants her to see the whole picture and also admits that missing freedom from expectations is real.

grounding: A family dialogue shows a teen under pressure longing for early childhood while forgetting its fears and limits.

passage: Last month, with three coaching tests a week, I kept opening old photos from when I was five: me in a yellow frock on our Hyderabad terrace, eating mango, laughing at nothing. I'd think, that girl had no worries at all. I missed her so much it hurt. Then, clearing my cupboard, I found my kindergarten drawing book. On one page, in wobbly letters, I had written "I am skared of thunder" beside a black cloud. Another page showed me alone at the gate, waiting for the school van, a tear drawn on my face. I sat on the floor for a long time. I told Aditi the next day. She said, "Maybe you miss being looked after, not being little." That felt right. I'm Zainab, and I still keep the mango photo on my wall, next to the thunder page.

qa.q: What had Zainab written beside the black cloud in the drawing book?
qa.a: "I am skared of thunder."

qa.q: Why did Zainab miss her five-year-old self so much during that month?
qa.a: The pressure of three coaching tests a week made the easy-looking photos feel like a lost comfort, so she saw only the laughter, not the fears.

qa.q: What did Zainab choose to do with the photo and the drawing, and why does it help?
qa.a: She kept the mango photo next to the thunder page, holding both the happy and the scared memories together.

qa.q: How did Aditi's view change the way Zainab saw her longing?
qa.a: Aditi suggested Zainab missed being looked after, not being little, which gave the feeling a clearer and kinder name.

grounding: A teenager under pressure remembers early childhood as carefree until she finds drawings that recall its fears.
